strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful approach to a difficult camera-geometry problem. Reusing five-point and P3P solvers makes the method substantially easier to implement than specialized algebraic or homotopy approaches.

The empirical support is substantial: 90,000 camera triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic geometry/noise experiments, and extensive ablations. Supplementary evaluation using all three camera pairs strengthens the evidence beyond the main pose metric.

The results demonstrate practical value. In Table 2, the fully enhanced mean-point-plus-shifts solver improves PhotoTourism AUC@10 from HC's 73.53 to 77.14. The simpler mean-point solver with refinement, filtering, and ENM nearly matches the correspondingly enhanced five-point baseline's accuracy, 76.16 versus 76.20, at 44.51 versus 56.52 ms.

The manuscript clearly explains why refinement and early non-minimal refitting matter, and acknowledges approximation bias. Reproducibility is supported by a source-code link, established solver libraries, specified experimental settings, and hyperparameter validation on a scene excluded from the main evaluation. These merits favor acceptance.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison with HC is confounded by initialization overhead. Section 8.3 reports approximately 45 ms of model/data loading per RANSAC run, which could be amortized across triplets. Table 4 actually reports faster standalone execution for HC than for the mean-point solver: 66.06 versus 83.92 microseconds. Consequently, the reported full-pipeline timings do not establish the same speed advantage when HC's data are already loaded.

The strongest speed–accuracy claims are insufficiently controlled against the enhanced five-point baseline. Figure 4 omits its refinement/filtering variants, although Table 2 shows these improve performance. On Cambridge, the fully enhanced shifted-mean solver achieves 66.95 AUC@10 versus 66.35 for five-point+P3P+R+F, but takes 81.98 versus 31.82 ms. This is a useful accuracy trade-off, rather than evidence of uniform efficiency superiority.

The theoretical guarantee concerns only the virtual correspondence's distance to an epipolar line, bounded by triangle size. It provides no corresponding pose-error bound or guarantee that refinement reaches the correct solution. Figure 9 confirms nonzero errors even without measurement noise, so reliability remains empirical and dependent on successful hypothesis generation and refinement.

Smaller reporting concerns remain. In Table 6, the Cambridge mean-point +R+F and +R+F+ENM rows exactly repeat the corresponding affine rows, including runtimes; these entries need clarification. Variation across repeated RANSAC runs is also unreported, limiting interpretation of small differences between closely performing variants.
